content: The mons pubis, also referred to as the mons veneris or simply the mons, is a soft, rounded mound of tissue located in women just above the external genitalia. This area is elevated due to the presence of a layer of subcutaneous fat, which serves to cushion and protect the underlying pubic bone. Anatomically, it is situated anterior to the symphysis pubis. The size and prominence of the mons pubis can vary depending on an individual's overall body fat composition. Following puberty, this region typically becomes covered with pubic hair. In human anatomy, the mons pubis transitions into the labia majora on either side, which are the larger external folds of the vulva. These folds border a central groove, often referred to as the cleft of Venus, which encloses the clitoris, vaginal opening, and other structures of the vulva. The fatty tissue of the mons pubis is highly responsive to estrogen. During puberty, the influence of this hormone leads to the development of a more pronounced mound in this area. This growth also causes the anterior portion of the labia majora to be pushed outward and away from the pubic bone, aligning more parallel to the ground when the individual is in a standing position.
